descripcion: Academic and professional caution in English is built from three habits at once: hedging the certainty of a claim, using the passive to remove the actor, and reporting impersonally so no one person owns the statement. It has been suggested that this may require further review is not one trick but three, fused into a single sentence.

cuadroReferencia.notaPie: Two layers together read as careful. Three in a row, in every sentence, reads as evasive — reserve the full stack for the claims that actually need it.

ejemplos.texto: It has been suggested that the results may not generalise beyond this sample.
It is thought that the delay was caused by a data issue, though this hasn't been confirmed.
The findings could arguably be explained by seasonal variation.

notas: Stacking all three on a verifiable fact reads as dishonest, not careful — reserve the full combination for claims that are genuinely uncertain.
It has been suggested distances the writer from a claim without naming who made it, which is useful when the source is unclear or sensitive.
One flat, unhedged sentence per paragraph keeps the writing from sounding permanently uncertain.

contraste.es: Spanish hedges mainly with the conditional and creo que, and uses the impersonal passive far less as an academic device – it prefers the impersonal se (se sugiere que) to stacking three distinct layers as English does. Spanish speakers tend to under-hedge in academic English because in Spanish one layer is usually enough.
contraste.de: German academic prose uses the passive and man extensively, so removing the actor is familiar. The lexical hedges are less graded than in English, and man is often calqued as one (one could argue that…), which sounds formal and old-fashioned in most English registers.
contraste.it: Italian academic prose hedges with the si impersonale and the condizionale (si ritiene che, sembrerebbe), and it is thought that matches si ritiene che well. The typical risk is stacking conditionals (it would seem that it could be…) where English uses one lexical hedge and a passive.
contraste.fr: French academic prose hedges with the conditionnel and on (on pourrait penser que, il semblerait que). The calque one could think that sounds stilted in English; it could be argued that or it would appear that is the natural equivalent.
contraste.pt: Portuguese hedges with the se impersonal (considera-se que) and, in European Portuguese, with the future (poderá indicar). The calque will indicate is far too certain in English; considera-se que maps well onto it is considered that.

errores: Stacking all three layers on a fact that is actually certain, which reads as evasive.
Using the passive without any hedge, which sounds more confident than the evidence supports.
Never using the full stack at all, so genuinely uncertain claims sound overstated.

traducciones.de: Es wurde die Vermutung geäußert, dass…

redemittel.expresion: This could arguably be explained by…

traducciones.de: Das ließe sich wohl durch… erklären.
traducciones.fr: Cela pourrait sans doute s’expliquer par…
traducciones.it: Questo potrebbe forse essere spiegato da…
traducciones.pt: Isto poderia, de certa forma, explicar-se por…

traducciones.fr: …, bien que cela reste à confirmer.

redemittel.expresion: There is some evidence to suggest that…
redemittel.funcion: names the type of support without overclaiming

traducciones.de: Es gibt einige Hinweise darauf, dass…
traducciones.it: Ci sono alcuni indizi che suggeriscono che…

autochequeo: Is the full three-layer stack reserved for claims that are genuinely uncertain?
Is there at least one flat, unhedged sentence to show the contrast?
Does the passive remove an actor that genuinely doesn't need naming?
Would a reader sense evasion rather than care anywhere in the text?
Are hedges varied, not the same word repeated every time?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the combination of hedging, passive and impersonal reporting. Flag any claim where all three layers are used but the fact is actually certain, and flag any certain claim left completely unhedged. Do not rewrite the text.

es: *parece ser que* rendered as *It seems to be that* instead of *It seems that*.
de: *eventuell* rendered as *eventually* in a hedge: *This could eventually cause delays* for 'possibly', where *eventually* means 'in the end'.
it: *si ritiene che* rendered as *It is retained that* instead of *It is believed that*.
fr: *on estime que* rendered as *One estimates that* instead of *It is estimated that*.
pt: *estima-se que* rendered as *It estimates that* instead of *It is estimated that*.
